newsitem.title: PERU: Meeting plans renew hope of new Peru crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Meeting plans renew hope of new Peru crisis talks.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages planned to meet with mediators on Sunday to discuss jump-starting talks with the government amid a report President Alberto Fujimori has offered to let most of the rebels stay in Peru.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said he expected a visit by members of a mediating panel looking to resume talks in the 82-day crisis, but could not say if or when rebels would return to the bargaining table.
"We'll wait for the guarantors commission to come here, talk to them and, at that point, we'll decide," he said in a walkie-talkie interview. "We are constantly evaluating the situation."

A Japanese daily reported on Sunday that the government had proposed that most of the approximately 20 rebels in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima could remain in the country if they released of all the hostages.

The Mainichi Shimbun quoted sources close to Fujimori and his negotiating team as saying the proposal was submitted on Wednesday during the last round of talks between the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

The paper said officials proposed letting most of the rebels remain in the country without prosecution, provided Cerpa and up to three others charged with prior offences went into exile in Cuba. It also offered to make prison and judicial reforms and change the way criminal investigations are undertaken.

The MRTA was to reply to the proposal in the 10th round of talks on Friday. But rebels abruptly called off the meeting, charging security forces planned to rescue the hostages in an attack on the besieged residence using secret tunnels being dug under the diplomatic compound.

As a foggy dawn broke on the hostages' 82nd day in captivity, rebels and security forces resumed their by-now routine dueling of revolutionary hymns and slogans versus traditional Peruvian music blared from police loudspeakers.

Local radio said groups from Lima's poor districts planned to march near the residence on Sunday while municipal officials on Peru's north coast planned a demonstration by up to 10,000 people to show their "solidarity" with the hostages.
With negotiations at a standstill, Roman Catholic church officials on Saturday urged both sides to resume talks and avoid bloodshed in ending Latin America's longest hostage siege.
"We can't let it reach the point of violence," Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora, archbishop of Lima and the head of Peru's Catholic Church, told reporters.
Both the rebels and Fujimori stated their wish to resume talks and Cerpa, in the interview on Saturday, said guarantors on Sunday would "make contact to proceed to a new dialogue."

But a gulf of mistrust still separates both sides. An MRTA spokeswoman said rebels, who seized the residence on Dec. 17, had heard strange noises for days underneath the building in Lima's upscale San Isidro district.

"We heard noises, not just for a moment but for several days. (At first) we didn't want to go public with this; we waited to find out for sure," said the guerrilla, who identified herself as Comrade Micaela in a two-way radio interview with Reuters.

Fujimori on Saturday continued to dodge questions about the tunnels while news reports said Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada was assured by Peruvian officials that no tunnels were being built. Bolivia's envoy to Lima is among the hostages.
The rebels are demanding the release of hundreds of jailed comrades. The government has steadfastly refused to consider the idea
Local radio quoted Cerpa as saying the two sides "still need to adjust some details" before renewing dialogue.
